narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. This signal of relative academic standing in law school carried the most weight.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 39, you scored above the average of 37.2 seen among accepted applicants, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the third most influential feature. It sat slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore nudged the outcome modestly toward failure.

Taken together, the model concluded that your lower law-school class standing outweighed the positive effect of your stronger LSAT, resulting in an overall risk of failure that led to rejection.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your law-school grades so your class rank rises. Stronger performance in the remaining years can directly address the factor that hurt your application most. Consider seeking academic support or study strategies that have helped other students climb in rank. With clearer evidence of improvement, a future application would be viewed more favorably.
